elements.quote: As of 23 March 2022, more than 475 million people have been infected with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)... Despite global efforts to identify effective interventions for the prevention and treatment of covid-19, which have resulted in approximately 3000 trials completed or underway, evidence for effective treatment remains limited.
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state of knowledge (large trial volume) and the key uncertainty (limited evidence for effective treatment) with citations.

elements.quote: Summarising the rapidly growing evidence base has been a challenge. Living systematic reviews deal with the main limitation of traditional reviews-that of providing an overview of the relevant evidence only at a specific time. This is crucial in the context of covid-19, in which the best evidence is constantly changing.
elements.reason: The need and importance of the review are explicitly explained in the context of a rapidly evolving evidence base and changing best evidence.

elements.quote: This living network meta-analysis is the fifth version. The previous versions are available in the supplementary material. Drugs for prophylaxis 9 and antibody-based treatments 10 are addressed separately.
elements.reason: As an update, the manuscript identifies this as the fifth version with previous versions cited, and the discussion (callout_2) also distinguishes it from two other similar efforts, explaining the need for this review.

elements.quote: Mounting evidence suggests that antivirals (such as molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir) are most effective in the early stages of covid-19 when patients have non-severe disease, whereas anti-inflammatories (such as corticosteroids) seem to be most effective in the later disease stages.
elements.reason: A brief mechanistic rationale (antivirals early vs anti-inflammatories late in disease) appears only in the strengths/limitations section as a future-direction justification, not in the introduction where the rationale for the interventions is described; hence partial.
This is a review of drug treatments (pharmacological interventions) for covid-19, not a complex intervention or complex delivery context, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: To compare the effects of treatments for coronavirus disease 2019 (covid-19).
elements.reason: The abstract contains an explicit objective statement clearly declaring the review's aim.

elements.quote: Randomised clinical trials in which people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 were randomised to drug treatment or to standard care or placebo.
elements.reason: Population (people with covid-19), interventions (drug treatments), and comparators (standard care or placebo) are identifiable, but the planned comparisons are not explicitly stated in PICO form alongside the objective; outcomes are described separately in the Data Collection section.

elements.quote: We included randomised clinical trials in people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 that compared drugs for treatment against one another or against no intervention, placebo, or standard care... No restrictions were applied based on severity of illness or setting
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria specify population (covid-19 patients), design (randomised trials), comparisons, and state no restrictions on setting or severity; follow-up not restricted.

elements.quote: We included trials regardless of publication status (peer reviewed, in press, or preprint) or language.
elements.reason: Explicitly states no restrictions on publication status or language; no year restrictions implied by comprehensive search.

elements.quote: Several trials could not be included in the analysis because both arms would have been classified within the same treatment node, they evaluated different durations or doses of the same drug, had insufficient data, or reported no outcomes of interest.
elements.reason: Distinguishes reasons for exclusion; 'had insufficient data' vs 'reported no outcomes of interest' and figure 1 excludes 'Randomised trial with no results', distinguishing measured vs reported outcomes, though not fully explicit.

elements.quote: For each outcome, interventions were classified in groups from the most to the least beneficial or harmful following GRADE guidance.
elements.reason: Grouping into nodes/classes is implied via treatment nodes and the at-least-100-patients/20-events analysis threshold, and interventions excluded are categorised separately (text_13), but the full list of synthesis groups/comparisons defined in the objectives is not explicitly specified in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: we decided to report evidence on treatments for which at least 100 people were randomised or for which there were at least 20 events... We include preprints because of the urgent need for information and because so many of the studies on covid-19 are published first as preprints.
elements.reason: Rationales are given for notable restrictions (analysis threshold for sparse data; inclusion of preprints; grouping placebo/standard care in same node).

elements.quote: We searched all English information sources from 1 December 2019 to 3 December 2021, and the Chinese literature from conception of the databases to 20 February 2021.
elements.reason: End dates for searching all sources are reported, including the stop date for Chinese databases (20 February 2021) and English sources (3 December 2021), with daily searches described for the living review.

elements.quote: Medline (Ovid and PubMed), PubMed Central, Embase, CAB Abstracts, Global Health, PsycInfo, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Academic Search Complete, Africa Wide Information, CINAHL, ProQuest Central, SciFinder, the Virtual Health Library, LitCovid...
elements.reason: Bibliographic databases are named, platforms/interfaces specified where relevant (e.g., Medline via Ovid and PubMed), and overall coverage dates (1 December 2019 to 3 December 2021) are given.

elements.quote: We perform daily searches from Monday to Friday in the World Health Organization (WHO) covid-19 database... These included the Living Overview of the Evidence (L-OVE) COVID-19 Repository by the Epistemonikos Foundation and the Systematic and Living Map on COVID-19 Evidence by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health
elements.reason: Registers and repositories (WHO covid-19 database including ClinicalTrials.gov, L-OVE, living evidence map) are named, with search dates reported (to 3 December 2021).

elements.quote: WHO covid-19 website, CDC covid-19 website
elements.reason: Websites (WHO and CDC covid-19 websites) are named as sources within the WHO database, but no URLs are reported.
No organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies are named in the methods; 'data from authors' appears only in results/figure without naming any organisation.
The methods do not describe any individuals contacted to identify studies; only the results figure mentions 'Data from authors' without describing who was contacted.

elements.quote: 5 Reference lists of published studies
elements.reason: The study selection figure (Fig 1, image figure_3) shows '5 Reference lists of published studies' as an external source, indicating reference lists were consulted, but the methods text does not specify the types of reference lists examined.
No backward or forward citation searching (seed reports, citation index/platform, or search date) is reported.
The figure lists '4 Presentations' as a source, but the methods do not report consultation of specific journals or conference proceedings with dates covered and search methods.

elements.quote: We adapted the search terms for covid-19 developed by the CDC to the Chinese language. ... The supplementary file includes the Chinese literature search strategy.
elements.reason: Sources and dates are described and a machine learning model filter for randomised trials is mentioned, but the full search strategies for the main English databases (e.g., WHO covid-19 database) are only referenced to supplementary material, not fully reported in the text.

elements.quote: The daily searches are designed to match the update schedule of the database and to capture eligible studies the day of or the day after publication. ... We searched all English information sources from 1 December 2019 to 3 December 2021, and the Chinese literature from conception of the databases to 20 February 2021.
elements.reason: Date limits and the trial-type filter are stated, and stopping of Chinese database searching is explained, but limits are not systematically tied to all eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: We adapted the search terms for covid-19 developed by the CDC to the Chinese language.
elements.reason: A published search approach (CDC covid-19 search terms) is cited and its adaptation to Chinese is described.
No natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms are reported.
No tools for translating search strings between sources are reported or implied.
No validation of the search strategy is described in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is described in the retrieved evidence.
No evidence indicates a non-PICO conceptual search structure was used; no reporting requirement applies.

elements.quote: Using a systematic review software, Covidence, 17 pairs of reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, independently screened all titles and abstracts, followed by full texts of trials that were identified as potentially eligible.
elements.reason: Reports number of reviewers (pairs of reviewers) for both title/abstract and full-text screening stages.

elements.quote: 17 pairs of reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, independently screened all titles and abstracts, followed by full texts
elements.reason: Explicitly states reviewers worked independently at both screening stages.

elements.quote: A third reviewer adjudicated conflicts.
elements.reason: Conflict resolution during study selection described (third reviewer adjudication).

elements.quote: One trial did not stratify reporting of outcomes for those who were truly randomised versus those who were allocated by preference; the authors shared outcome data with us among patients who were truly randomised.
elements.reason: Contacting investigators for eligibility information is not explicitly described; only data sharing for outcomes is reported. No process for obtaining/confirming eligibility information from investigators is reported, though external sources (data from authors) appear in the flow diagram.

elements.quote: Our search strategy and eligibility criteria were comprehensive, without restrictions on language of publication or publication status.
elements.reason: No mention of translated abstracts or articles; with no language restrictions and no evidence translation was needed, this requirement does not apply based on available evidence.

elements.quote: Using a systematic review software, Covidence, 17 pairs of reviewers...independently screened all titles and abstracts
elements.reason: Use of Covidence systematic review software in the screening process is described.
No externally derived classifiers identified or described in the retrieved evidence; the flow diagram (figure_3) shows excluded records but no classifier-based removal is reported.
No internally derived machine-learning classifier is mentioned anywhere in the retrieved evidence, so this requirement does not apply.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping rules for screening are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No crowdsourcing platforms are mentioned in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Searches of living evidence retrieval services identified 219 publications of eligible randomised trials, which were reconciled with our formal search strategy when necessary.
elements.reason: Previously screened datasets from living evidence retrieval services (e.g., Epistemonikos, per figure_3) were used and reconciled with the formal search, but details of how these datasets were derived are not fully described.

elements.quote: For each eligible trial, pairs of reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, extracted data independently using a standardised, pilot tested data extraction form.
elements.reason: Data were extracted by pairs of reviewers.

elements.quote: pairs of reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, extracted data independently
elements.reason: Independent data extraction is explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Reviewers resolved discrepancies by discussion and, when necessary, with adjudication by a third party.
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution process (discussion then third-party adjudication) is described.
No evidence of contacting study investigators to obtain or confirm data.
No automation tools for data extraction are described; a standardised data extraction form was used.
No reporting of translation methods for data collection.
No software for extracting data from figures is specified.

Preprint updates and a hierarchy for the mechanical ventilation outcome are mentioned, but no general decision rules for selecting among multiple reports of the same study or resolving inconsistencies between reports are described.

elements.quote: Selected outcomes included mortality (closest to 90 days), mechanical ventilation (total number of patients, over 90 days), adverse events leading to discontinuation (within 28 days), admission to hospital, length of hospital stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and time to symptom resolution or clinical improvement.
elements.reason: Lists the outcome domains for which data were sought, with definitions (e.g., mechanical ventilation includes invasive and non-invasive; CPAP/BiPAP considered non-invasive).

elements.quote: mortality (closest to 90 days), mechanical ventilation (total number of patients, over 90 days), adverse events leading to discontinuation (within 28 days)
elements.reason: Time frames are given for mortality, mechanical ventilation, and adverse events, but not explicitly for admission to hospital, length of stay, or time to symptom resolution.

elements.quote: Outcomesofinterestwereselectedbasedonimportancetopatients 18 and were informed by clinical expertise... All panel members rated outcomes from 1 to 9 based on importance to individual patients (9 being most important), and we included any outcome rated 7 or higher by any panel member.
elements.reason: Describes the process for selecting which outcomes were included, implying that not all compatible results were collected, but does not explicitly state whether all compatible results within each outcome domain (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. We used the number of patients ventilated at the time point that the largest number of the patients were ventilated, if the trial reported the number of patients ventilated at specific timepoints.
elements.reason: Describes the method used to decide which results to collect for mechanical ventilation when not all compatible results were used.

elements.quote: In contrast to previous iterations, for this iteration, we did not include several outcomes which the GDG did not think were critical to decision making: viral clearance (closest to 7 days, 3 days either way), time to viral clearance, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, and days free from mechanical ventilation (within 28 days).
elements.reason: Reports changes to outcome-domain inclusion across iterations with the rationale (GDG did not consider them critical to decision making).

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study.
elements.reason: The hierarchy for selecting results within the mechanical ventilation domain is described, and the strengths/limitations section (text_26) gives a rationale, but the methods text does not explicitly frame it as a change to the result-selection process with rationale for the change.

elements.quote: Outcomesofinterestwereselectedbasedonimportancetopatients 18 and were informed by clinical expertise in the systematic review teamandinthelinkedguidelinepanel... All panel members rated outcomes from 1 to 9 based on importance to individual patients (9 being most important), and we included any outcome rated 7 or higher by any panel member.
elements.reason: Explains that outcomes were prioritised based on importance to patients, with the rating process (7 or higher by panel members) serving as the rationale for prioritisation.

elements.quote: Reviewers collected information on trial characteristics (trial registration, publication status, study status, design), patient characteristics (country, age, sex, smoking habits, comorbidities, setting and type of care, and severity of covid-19 symptoms for studies of treatment), and outcomesofinterest (means or medians and measures of variability for continuous outcomes and the number of participants analysed and the number of participants who experienced an event for dichotomous outcomes).
elements.reason: The Data Collection section lists and defines the trial and participant characteristics and outcome data items sought, with further specification of selected outcomes (mortality, ventilation, adverse events, etc.).

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. ... Weused author definitions for mechanical ventilation; when separate, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) were considered non-invasive mechanical ventilation.
elements.reason: The authors describe assumptions/decisions for handling unclear or inconsistently reported information (a hierarchy for mechanical ventilation, use of author definitions, counting CPAP/BiPAP as non-invasive ventilation, and updating preprint data when peer-reviewed versions appeared).

elements.quote: Outcomesofinterestwereselectedbasedonimportancetopatients 18 and were informed by clinical expertise in the systematic review teamandinthelinkedguidelinepanelresponsiblefortheWHOBMJ Rapid Recommendations.
elements.reason: A cited source (reference 18, a patient-important outcomes study) and the WHO/BMJ Rapid Recommendations panel rating process (outcomes rated 7 or higher) were used to determine which data items (outcomes) to collect.

elements.quote: used a revision of the Cochrane tool for assessing risk of bias in randomised trials (RoB 2.0) 20 to rate trials
elements.reason: The tool used (RoB 2.0, with reference citation 20) is clearly specified.

elements.quote: across the following domains: bias arising from the randomisation process; bias owing to departures from the intended intervention; bias from missing outcome data; bias in measurement of the outcome; bias in selection of the reported results, including deviations from the registered protocol; bias due to competing risks; and bias arising from early termination for benefit.
elements.reason: All domains assessed by the tool are explicitly enumerated.

elements.quote: We rated trials at high risk of bias overall if one or more domains were rated as probably high risk of bias or as high risk of bias and as low risk of bias if all domains were rated as probably low risk of bias or low risk of bias.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement is made and the derivation rules are reported.

elements.quote: Risk of bias of the included studies was assessed using a modification of the Cochrane risk of bias 2.0 tool
elements.reason: A modification of the RoB 2.0 tool is acknowledged (text_17 lists additional domains such as competing risks and early termination), but the adaptations are not described as such in detail or justified.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is described or made publicly accessible in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, used a revision of the Cochrane tool ... Reviewers resolved discrepancies by discussion and, when not possible, with adjudication by a third party.
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution via discussion and third-party adjudication is reported, but the exact number of reviewers per study and their independence are not explicitly stated for risk-of-bias assessment.
No processes for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators are described.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence; manual assessment is described.

elements.quote: We summarised the effect of interventions on dichotomous outcomes using the odds ratio and corresponding 95% credible interval. For continuous outcomes, we used the mean difference ... For time to symptom resolution, we first performed the analyses using the relative effect measure ratio of means ... before calculating the mean difference in days
elements.reason: The Summary Measures section explicitly specifies effect measures for each outcome type (odds ratio, mean difference, ratio of means).

elements.quote: To evaluate certainty of no benefit (or no effect), we used a 2% risk difference threshold of the 95% credible interval for mortality and mechanical ventilation. In other words, if the entire 95% credible interval was within 2% of the null effect, we would not rate down for imprecision. We decided on this preliminary threshold based on a survey of the authors.
elements.reason: A threshold (2% risk difference) with rationale is reported, but only for imprecision judgments on two outcomes in the certainty assessment; general thresholds for interpreting effect sizes are not comprehensively reported, though a minimally contextualised framework with null effect as threshold of importance is mentioned.

elements.quote: To facilitate interpretation of the results, we calculated absolute effects for outcomes in which the summary measure was an odds ratio or ratio of means. ... We calculated absolute effects using the transitive risks model 33 using R2jags package in R.
elements.reason: Re-expression of results as absolute effects from relative measures (odds ratio, ratio of means) is described, including the method (transitive risks model) and data sources for baseline risks; text_19 also describes converting ratio of means to mean difference.

elements.quote: we used the mean difference and corresponding 95% credible interval in days for ICU length of stay, length of hospital stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation because we expected similar durations across randomised trials ... because we expected substantial variation between studies
elements.reason: The choice of effect measures is justified (expected similar durations across trials; expected substantial variation between studies motivating ratio of means).

elements.quote: Several trials could not be included in the analysis because both arms would have been classified within the same treatment node, they evaluated different durations or doses of the same drug, had insufficient data, or reported no outcomes of interest. Ultimately, we analysed 265 (63%) trials that reported on treatments with at least 100 patients or 20 events.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes how studies were assigned to syntheses: trials excluded from analysis when both arms fell in the same treatment node, evaluated different doses/durations, or had insufficient data/outcomes; a threshold of at least 100 patients or 20 events was applied for inclusion in analysis (also stated in callout_2), and the flow diagram (text_26, figure_3) shows exclusions leading to the 265 trials analysed versus 43 for the next update.

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. We used the number of patients ventilated at the time point that the largest number of the patients were ventilated, if the trial reported the number of patients ventilated at specific timepoints. We used author definitions for mechanical ventilation; when separate, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) were considered non-invasive mechanical ventilation.
elements.reason: The methods describe data preparation steps: a hierarchy for handling inconsistent reporting of mechanical ventilation, definitions/conversions for ventilation types (CPAP/BiPAP as non-invasive), and elsewhere (text_21, text_9) rules for excluding sparse treatment nodes (>=100 patients or >=20 events) and combining placebo/standard care arms into one node, covering preparation of data for synthesis.

The retrieved evidence shows results being displayed (e.g., Table 1 study characteristics, supplementary tables of effect estimates), but nowhere in the Methods do the authors describe the tabular structures used to display results of individual studies or syntheses.
Figures such as network plots (Fig S1) and Figure 2 summary of effects appear in the results/supplements, but the Methods do not describe any graphical methods used to display results.

elements.quote: For each outcome, interventions were classified in groups from the most to the least beneficial or harmful following GRADE guidance.
elements.reason: This describes ordering of interventions in the synthesis, but there is no explicit description of the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs; the ordering rationale for study-level tabular/graphical displays is not reported.

No non-standard graphs are described in the retrieved evidence, and no rationale for the use of any non-standard graphical displays is provided; the evidence does not support a conclusion that this does not apply.

elements.quote: All network meta-analyses were performed using the gemtc package of R version 3.6.3 (RStudio, Boston, MA) 26 and all pairwise meta-analyses using the bayesmeta package.
elements.reason: Software packages (gemtc, bayesmeta, R2jags/JAGS in reference 34) and R version 3.6.3 are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: For most outcomes, we conducted network meta-analyses and pairwise meta-analyses using a bayesian framework
elements.reason: Meta-analysis was performed, so an alternative synthesis method description is not applicable.

elements.quote: In previous versions, we used fixed effects for some outcomes because data was sparse or dominated by a single trial. As per our protocol, we used random effects for all outcomes.
elements.reason: The model (Bayesian random-effects) and rationale for the choice are reported.

elements.quote: For all analyses, we used three Markov chains with 100 000 iterations after an initial burn-in of 10 000 and a thinning of 10. We used node splitting models to assess local incoherence and to obtain indirect estimates.
elements.reason: Statistical methods (Bayesian MCMC estimation, node splitting for indirect estimates/incoherence) are described.

elements.quote: We used a plausible prior for variance parameter and a uniform prior for the effect parameter suggested in a previous study based on empirical data.
elements.reason: Heterogeneity is handled and quantified via an empirically informed prior on the between-study variance parameter; incoherence assessed with node splitting.

elements.quote: the same priors for the variance and effect parameters... We used a plausible prior for variance parameter
elements.reason: The between-study variance is modeled via a specified empirical prior in the Bayesian framework.

elements.quote: The minimally contextualised approachconsidersonlywhethercredibleintervals include the null effect
